Secondary Diminished Chords: Practice for Chapter 18

Exercises for Chapter 18 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: secondary leading-tone chords (vii°/x, viiø7/x, vii°7/x) in major and minor, analysing and writing them with figures 6, 64, 65, 43, 42, lead-sheet symbols, and the book’s listening examples.

This page goes with Chapter 18, Secondary Diminished Chords of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows Chapter 17, Secondary Dominants, and uses the seventh-chord qualities of Chapter 8.

Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. ▶ Hear it plays the chord and then the chord it resolves to.

Typing a secondary diminished chord: vii°/V, vii°7/ii, viiø7/IV. Type o (or dim) for °, and h (or Ø) for ø. After the slash comes the chord being tonicized, and its case is its quality: ii is minor, IV is major. Inversions take the figures the book uses: vii°6/V and vii°64/V for triads, viiø65/V, vii°43/iv and vii°42/vi for seventh chords. vii°6/5/V and vii°7 of iv work too.

18.1 Secondary diminished chords

In Chapter 9, vii° is a dominant-function chord, like V: it leads to the tonic. So a leading-tone chord can be borrowed for any major or minor chord of the key, just as V was in Chapter 17. It sits a half step below the chord it tonicizes, and it can be a diminished triad, a half-diminished seventh (ø7) or a fully-diminished seventh (°7). It is written vii°/x, viiø7/x or vii°7/x. Its chromatic note is part of the chord, not a passing decoration. Read 18.1

NoteListen: the book’s examples

Start with the symbols. Given the numeral in C, G or F major, which chord is it?

18.2 In major and minor

Which seventh chord? The book’s rule: a minor chord is tonicized by a fully-diminished seventh (vii°7/ii in C is C♯–E–G–B♭), and a major chord is usually tonicized by a half-diminished seventh (viiø7/V in C is F♯–A–C–E), though °7 is also found before major chords. That matches the key each target would be the tonic of: vii°7 belongs to harmonic minor, viiø7 to major. Read 18.2

C major: tonicized vii°/x vii7/x C minor: tonicized vii°/x vii7/x
ii (Dm) C♯° C♯°7 III (E♭) (D° = ii°) (Dø7 = iiø7)
iii (Em) D♯° D♯°7 iv (Fm) E° E°7
IV (F) E° Eø7 V (G) F♯° F♯°7
V (G) F♯° F♯ø7 VI (A♭) G° Gø7
vi (Am) G♯° G♯°7 VII (B♭) A° Aø7

Diminished chords are not tonicized, as in Chapter 17. In minor, the chords for III use only the key’s notes: the triad is ii°, which the book leaves out, and the seventh chord is iiø7, which the book lists but notes that it has no accidentals and is told apart from iiø7 only by where it goes (iiø7 goes to V, viiø7/III to III). The drills leave both out, since on the staff they can’t be told from ii° and iiø7. Every other chord in the table has an accidental.

18.3 Analysing secondary diminished chords

The book’s two steps for a chord with a chromatic note:

  1. Stack it in thirds to find the root and the quality. If it isn’t a diminished triad, a half-diminished seventh or a fully-diminished seventh, it isn’t a secondary diminished chord.
  2. Go up a minor 2nd from the root. If that note is the root of a major or minor chord in the key, the chord is vii of that chord.

The book’s example: in D major, a G♯ half-diminished seventh with B in the bass (first inversion). A minor 2nd above G♯ is A, the root of V, so the chord is viiø65/V. Read 18.3

The chord on the staff is followed by the chord it tonicizes. Name the first one:

With inversions. Read the bass note to choose the figure:

18.4 Writing secondary diminished chords

The book’s procedure, worked here for vii°43/ii in E♭ major (the book’s own example is a different chord):

  1. Find the root of the chord after the slash: ii in E♭ is F (F minor).
  2. Go down a minor 2nd: E (E natural, not E♭).
  3. Build the chord there. F minor is minor, so fully diminished: E–G–B♭–D♭.
  4. Put it in the inversion asked for. 43 means the 5th is in the bass: B♭–D♭–E–G.

NoteFor teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
  • Chords drilled: the book’s Figures 18.2.1 and 18.2.2. vii°/x of every major and minor triad of the key (major ii iii IV V vi, minor iv V VI VII); vii°7 before a minor triad, viiø7 before a major one. A chord made only of the key’s notes is left out, as on the Chapter 17 page: vii°/III in minor (ii°, which the book leaves out too) and viiø7/III in minor (iiø7, which the book lists). vii°7 before a major chord, which the book says also occurs, is not drilled: the drills keep to the book’s tables so that each question has one answer.
  • Resolution: the naming drill always shows and plays the chord’s resolution (to the chord it names), in root position.
  • Voicing: close position above the bass. The drills are for spelling and labelling, not for voice leading.
  • Checked: node tests/lessons/secdim-drill.test.js generates thousands of questions and checks each one by its own arithmetic. The root must be a half step below the resolution’s root, the quality must be the one the tables give, the figure must match the bass, at least one note must be chromatic, and the drawn notes must match the answer.
  • Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube. The “Friends in Low Places” link the book uses is a recording on a “Brooks Jefferson” channel, not Garth Brooks’s own channel.
  • The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
